title: Conditional probability and Bayes' rule
summary: Compute probabilities given a condition, turn them around with Bayes' rule, and build a small naive Bayes text classifier with add-one smoothing.

sources.section: 6.3 Sum Rule, Product Rule, and Bayes' Theorem

license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner

steps.title: A positive test
steps.body:
A test for a rare illness is 99% accurate on people who have it and 95% accurate on people who don't.
You test positive. How worried should you be? Most people guess about 95%. The true answer, for an
illness that 1 person in 100 has, is about 17%. The gap is the difference between "the chance of a
positive test if ill" and "the chance of being ill if the test is positive", and Bayes' rule is how to
get from one to the other.

steps.title: Shrinking the world to the condition
steps.body:
A **conditional probability** `P(A | B)` is the chance of `A` among only the cases where `B` happened:
cross out everything else, then count. Of 10,000 people, 100 are ill and 99 of them test positive; of the
9,900 who are well, 5% (495) test positive too. Among the 594 positives, only 99 are ill: 1 in 6.

**Bayes' rule** does that bookkeeping in one line: `P(ill | +) = P(+ | ill) · P(ill) / P(+)`, where
`P(+)` adds up the positives from both groups. The rare base rate, the **prior**, matters as much as the
test's accuracy. Events are **independent** if knowing one doesn't change the chance of the other,
`P(A | B) = P(A)`.

**Naive Bayes** classifies a message by applying the rule to every word at once, *as if* the words were
independent given the class. They aren't, which is the "naive" part, but the scores often still rank the
classes well.

questions: If the illness were common (half of all people), what would P(ill | positive) be with the same test?
Why is P(positive | ill) not the same as P(ill | positive)?

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Conditional probability:** `P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)`, defined when `P(B) > 0`; from data, count the
cases with both and divide by the cases with `B`.

**Bayes' rule:** `P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B)`, with `P(B) = P(B | A) P(A) + P(B | not A) P(not A)` (the
sum rule). For a test: `P(+ | ill)` is the **sensitivity**, `P(− | well)` the **specificity**, so
`P(+ | well) = 1 − specificity`.

**Checking by simulation:** `rng.random()` is uniform on `[0, 1)`, so `rng.random() < p` is true with
probability `p`; repeating a seeded experiment many times and counting estimates any of these probabilities.

**Naive Bayes for words:** for each class `c`, the prior `P(c)` is its share of the training documents.
For a word `w`, **add-one smoothing** gives `P(w | c) = (count of w in class c + 1) / (words in class c + V)`,
where `V` is the number of distinct training words, so a word never seen in a class doesn't make the
whole product 0. A document's score for `c` is `log P(c) + Σ log P(w | c)` over its words (repeats count
each time; words outside the training vocabulary are skipped). Logs turn a product of many small
numbers into a sum that doesn't underflow. Predict by finding the highest score: every class whose score is
within `1e-9` of it counts as tied, and this lesson chooses the first of those in sorted order.

steps.title: Run it: the positive test, worked and simulated
steps.body: Bayes' rule with a 1% prior, 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity, then 100,000 simulated people as a check.
steps.code:
import random

prior, sensitivity, specificity = 0.01, 0.99, 0.95
p_positive = sensitivity * prior + (1 - specificity) * (1 - prior)
print('P(positive) =', round(p_positive, 4))
print('P(ill | positive) =', round(sensitivity * prior / p_positive, 4))

rng = random.Random(7)
positives = ill_and_positive = 0
for _ in range(100_000):
    ill = rng.random() < prior
    positive = rng.random() < (sensitivity if ill else 1 - specificity)
    if positive:
        positives += 1
        ill_and_positive += ill
print('simulated:', positives, 'positives,', ill_and_positive, 'of them ill:', round(ill_and_positive / positives, 4))
steps.expected_output:
P(positive) = 0.0594
P(ill | positive) = 0.1667
simulated: 5947 positives, 1018 of them ill: 0.1712

steps.title: Your turn: conditioning and Bayes' rule
steps.body:
Complete two functions.

`posterior(prior, sensitivity, specificity)` returns `P(ill | positive)` by Bayes' rule. Raise
`ValueError` if any argument is outside `[0, 1]`, or if a positive result is impossible (`P(+) = 0`).

`p_given(pairs, a, b)` takes observations `(x, y)` and returns the fraction of those with `y == b` that
also have `x == a`, as a float. Raise `ValueError` if no observation has `y == b`.
hints: `evidence = sensitivity * prior + (1 - specificity) * (1 - prior)`; the answer is `sensitivity * prior / evidence`.
`given = [x for x, y in pairs if y == b]`, then `given.count(a) / len(given)`.

tests.name: the positive test
tests.code:
got = posterior(0.01, 0.99, 0.95)
assert isinstance(got, float) and abs(got - 0.0099 / 0.0594) <= 1e-12, f'99 of the 594 positives are ill: 1/6; got {got!r}'

tests.name: the prior matters
tests.code:
for prior, sens, spec in ((0.5, 0.99, 0.95), (0.001, 0.99, 0.95), (0.2, 0.8, 0.9), (0.3, 0.6, 0.7)):
    want = sens * prior / (sens * prior + (1 - spec) * (1 - prior))
    got = posterior(prior, sens, spec)
    assert abs(got - want) <= 1e-12, f'prior={prior}, sensitivity={sens}, specificity={spec}: {want}; got {got}'
assert posterior(0.5, 0.99, 0.95) > 0.95 > posterior(0.01, 0.99, 0.95), 'the same test means much more when the illness is common'

tests.name: edge cases
tests.code:
assert posterior(1, 0.7, 0.2) == 1.0, 'if everyone is ill, a positive person is ill'
assert posterior(0, 0.9, 0.5) == 0.0, 'if nobody is ill, nobody positive is'
assert posterior(0.3, 0.8, 1) == 1.0, 'with perfect specificity there are no false positives'
assert posterior(0.4, 0, 0.5) == 0.0
for args, want in (((0.3, 1, 0), 0.3), ((0.2, 1, 0.9), 0.2 / (0.2 + 0.1 * 0.8)), ((0.4, 0.7, 0), 0.28 / (0.28 + 0.6))):
    got = posterior(*args)
    assert abs(got - want) <= 1e-12, f'posterior{args} is valid: {want}; got {got}'

tests.name: conditioning on data
tests.code:
pairs = [('rain', 'cloudy'), ('dry', 'cloudy'), ('dry', 'sunny'), ('rain', 'cloudy')]
assert p_given(pairs, 'rain', 'cloudy') == 2 / 3
assert p_given(pairs, 'rain', 'sunny') == 0.0 and p_given(pairs, 'dry', 'sunny') == 1.0
got = p_given([(1, 'x'), (2, 'y'), (1, 'y'), (1, 'y'), (3, 'y')], 1, 'y')
assert isinstance(got, float) and got == 0.5, f'2 of the 4 with y == "y"; got {got!r}'

tests.name: independence
tests.code:
pairs = [(a, b) for a in ('h', 't') for b in (1, 2, 3)] * 2
assert p_given(pairs, 'h', 2) == 0.5, 'a coin and a die: knowing the die says nothing about the coin'

tests.name: inputs are not changed
tests.code:
pairs = [('a', 1), ('b', 1)]
keep = list(pairs)
p_given(pairs, 'a', 1)
assert pairs == keep

tests.name: bad input

steps.title: Challenge: a naive Bayes spam filter
steps.body:
Write three functions by the precise rules. `fit_nb(docs, labels)` learns from documents (each a list of
words) and their labels and returns a model in any form you like; raise `ValueError` if there are no
documents or `docs` and `labels` differ in length. `nb_scores(model, doc)` returns a dictionary from each
class to its log score for `doc`. `predict_nb(model, doc)` returns the best class, with the lesson's tie
rule. Don't change the inputs.
hints: Store the vocabulary, each class's prior, its word counts and its total number of words.

Score with `math.log(prior)` plus `math.log((count + 1) / (total + V))` for every known word; to predict, take `top = max(scores.values())` and the smallest class with a score of at least `top - 1e-9`.

tests.name: scores with add-one smoothing
repeated words in training documents count
predictions
a word unseen in one class
unknown words are skipped, repeats count
ties go to the first class in sorted order
tests.code:
m = fit_nb([['a'], ['b']], ['y', 'x'])
assert predict_nb(m, ['zzz']) == 'x', 'equal priors, nothing known: x sorts first'
m = fit_nb([['a', 'b'], ['b', 'a']], [2, 10])
assert predict_nb(m, ['a']) == 2, 'numbers sort as numbers'
m = fit_nb([['s', 's'], ['r', 'r']], ['beta', 'alpha'])
assert predict_nb(m, ['p', 'q', 'r', 's']) == 'alpha', 'the two scores are equal in exact arithmetic but can differ in the last digit: within 1e-9 they tie, so alpha'

tests.name: the 1e-9 tie tolerance
tests.code:
near = fit_nb([['x'] * 63246 + ['y'], ['x'] * 63245 + ['y']], ['zed', 'abe'])
s = nb_scores(near, ['x'])
assert 0 < s['zed'] - s['abe'] < 1e-9, 'zed scores about 5e-10 higher'
assert predict_nb(near, ['x']) == 'abe', 'within 1e-9 the scores tie, so the first class in sorted order wins'
far = fit_nb([['x'] * 20001 + ['y'], ['x'] * 20000 + ['y']], ['zed', 'abe'])
s = nb_scores(far, ['x'])
assert 1e-9 < s['zed'] - s['abe'] < 1e-8 and predict_nb(far, ['x']) == 'zed', 'about 5e-9 apart: a real difference, so the higher score wins'
n = 57735
three = fit_nb([['x'] * n + ['y'], ['x'] * (n + 1) + ['y'], ['x'] * (n + 2) + ['y']], ['abe', 'bob', 'cid'])
s = nb_scores(three, ['x'])
assert 1e-9 < s['cid'] - s['abe'] < 2e-9 and 0 < s['cid'] - s['bob'] < 1e-9, 'scores about 6e-10 apart, in order abe, bob, cid'
assert predict_nb(three, ['x']) == 'bob', 'cid is highest; bob is within 1e-9 of it and abe is not, so the tie is bob and cid: bob'

tests.name: long messages don't underflow
empty training documents
more than two classes
tests.code:
docs = [['goal', 'match'], ['vote', 'law'], ['film', 'actor'], ['goal', 'team'], ['law', 'court']]
labels = ['sport', 'politics', 'arts', 'sport', 'politics']
m = fit_nb(docs, labels)
assert set(nb_scores(m, ['goal'])) == {'sport', 'politics', 'arts'}
assert [predict_nb(m, d) for d in (['goal'], ['court'], ['actor', 'film'])] == ['sport', 'politics', 'arts']

questions.prompt: Of 20 cloudy days it rained on 8, and of 30 sunny days on 3. What is P(rain | cloudy)?
A test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific; 1 person in 100 is ill. Roughly what is P(ill | positive)?
questions.explanation: The many healthy people produce more false positives (495 in 10,000) than the few ill people produce true ones (99).

questions.prompt: Why does naive Bayes add 1 to every word count?
choices: So a word never seen in a class doesn't make that class's probability 0
To include unknown words in the vocabulary
questions.explanation: Without smoothing a single unseen word would rule a class out entirely.

questions.prompt: Why add log probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?
choices: A product of many small numbers underflows to 0; the sum of logs doesn't
questions.explanation: The ranking is the same, because log is increasing, and the numbers stay usable.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Compute a conditional probability by restricting to the condition and counting.
- Turn `P(B | A)` into `P(A | B)` with Bayes' rule, and explain why the prior matters.
- Build a naive Bayes classifier with add-one smoothing and log scores.
- Say what "naive" assumes, and why the classifier works anyway.
